corrections.form_value: The paper calls only the audience viewers' clip allocation randomized.
corrections.source_says: Too narrow. The paper also says clip order was randomized within each evaluation stream, and that includes the five experts, not only the viewers. Every randomization statement concerns the raters (abstract; p. 6, Sections 3.5.3 and 3.7). None says how practitioners were assigned. Suggested wording: 'The paper calls randomized only the rating side: the viewers' clip allocation and presentation, and clip order in both the expert and audience streams.' No code changes.
corrections.quote: Condition labels were concealed from both expert and audience raters, and clip order was randomized within each evaluation stream.

corrections.source_says: Same issue. The paper also randomized clip order in the expert rating stream. Suggested wording: 'randomization is stated only for the raters (the viewers' clip allocation and presentation, and clip order in both rating streams)'. Criterion 1 stays unclear.
corrections.quote: Condition labels were concealed from both expert and audience raters, and clip order was randomized within each evaluation stream.

confirmed: Version: Frontiers in Computer Science 8:1832169, doi 10.3389/fcomp.2026.1832169. Received 16 March 2026, revised 27 April 2026, accepted 29 April 2026, published 28 May 2026. 12 pages. Title and the four authors match (p. 1, masthead and citation box).

Supplement: URL on p. 11 (Supplementary material). The PDF does not include it. It holds deidentified expert and audience rating data, AHP weight tables, AHP matrix summaries, group-assignment tables, audience assignment summaries, and prompt metadata (p. 10, Data availability statement; p. 5, Section 3.4).

Assignment quote is verbatim: 20 practitioners, 10 assigned to baseline and 10 to package. The paper never says how they were assigned. The full text uses 'random' only for the raters (abstract; p. 6, Sections 3.5.3 and 3.7) and for model terms. randomized = not_stated is right (p. 5, Section 3.5.1).
No preregistration is mentioned anywhere in the 12 pages. preregistered = not_stated is right.

Participants quote is verbatim: one clip per practitioner, 20 clips, 10 per condition (p. 5, Section 3.4; p. 6, Section 3.6). No exclusions are reported, so 20 people were analyzed. Criterion 2 is not met (20 < 50).

Practitioner details match: mean age 32.05 (SD 4.26), 10 male and 10 female, animation 7, visual communication 7, motion design 6, experience 5.65 (baseline) vs 5.08 years (package) (p. 5, Section 3.5.1).

Both conditions used GPT-4o for ideation and prompt development and Sora for video generation. The only planned difference was the Kano-AHP worksheet (p. 4, Section 3.2; p. 5, Section 3.4; p. 6, Section 3.6). Both arms are generative_ai, and the contrast is a workflow, not AI versus no AI.

Raters: five experts rated every clip on all five dimensions (pp. 5-6, Section 3.5.2). 60 viewers each rated eight clips, 24 audience evaluations per clip (p. 1, abstract; p. 6, Section 3.5.3). The scale has 7 points (p. 6, Section 3.7).
Task: clips of 10 s, 1,080 x 1,920 pixels, 24 fps, 9:16 (p. 6, Section 3.6). Single bounded production session and one to three prompt versions per final clip (p. 4, Section 3.2).

S1-O1 reported string matches digit for digit: expert narrative coherence 3.92 (0.83) vs 5.04 (1.14), difference 1.12, g 1.11; beta 1.12, 95% CI [0.73, 1.51], Holm p <0.001 (p. 8, Tables 2 and 3; PDF text layer and page image).
S1-O2 reported string matches: expert emotional expressiveness 3.68 (0.96) vs 4.98 (1.00), difference 1.30, g 1.32; beta 1.30 [0.93, 1.67], p <0.001 (p. 8, Tables 2 and 3).
S1-O3 reported string matches: audience narrative coherence 4.12 (1.16) vs 4.96 (1.11), difference 0.84, g 0.74; beta 0.84 [0.65, 1.03], p <0.001 (p. 8, Tables 2 and 3).

One-line finding matches: package higher on all five dimensions in both rater groups. Expert g from 0.98 (visual style consistency) to 1.32 (emotional expressiveness). Audience g from 0.74 (narrative coherence) to 0.99 (motion smoothness) (p. 8, Table 2; p. 1, abstract; p. 7, Sections 4.1 to 4.5).

The five rated dimensions are quality dimensions. No novelty, originality, or overall creativity rating exists (p. 6, Section 3.7). So usefulness and other are fitting construct codes. Criterion 3 is met through the codebook's quality (usefulness) construct.
primary = not_stated is defensible: H1 to H5 cover all five dimensions equally (p. 2), and only the artifact reports are called exploratory (p. 6, Section 3.7).

Three outcomes, each with one contrast holding only reported and locator, is what the small-experiment short form asks for (tools/creativity-light.js). The other seven dimension-by-rater outcomes (p. 8, Tables 2 and 3) and the exploratory artifact-report rate (39/240 vs 25/240, chi-square(1) = 3.05, p = 0.081; p. 7, Section 4.4) are not required.
No company involvement: funded by the 2026 Hongik University Innovation Support Program Fund; no commercial conflict (p. 11, Funding and Conflict of interest).

Eligibility codes are right: core no, criterion 1 unclear, criterion 2 not_met, criterion 3 met, context_class none. Practitioner assignment is never called random, and even a random assignment would compare two workflows that both use generative AI with 20 people.
summary: The form matches the full text on design, counts (20 practitioners, 10 per arm, all analyzed; 5 experts and 60 viewers are raters), every number in the three reported strings and the one-line finding, and the eligibility codes, and no study randomly assigns people to generative-AI assistance. Three wording fixes change no code: two fields say randomization is stated only for the viewers, but the paper also randomized clip order for the experts (p. 6, Section 3.7), and the form says raters did not use AI, which the paper does not state.
